title: Cleaning a river
hookLine: volunteers cleaned the Kali Bein, the river where Nanak disappeared, by kar seva
last: TASVEER — A PAINTING, NOT A PHOTO.

cards: Mud up to the knees. A line of volunteers stands in a narrow, choked stream, passing buckets of black silt and tangled weeds from hand to hand up the bank. Some are farmers, some are students, some came after work.
Nobody is paid. The water barely moves, and it smells. But the stories of Guru Nanak know this stream.
It's the Kali Bein, at Sultanpur Lodhi, where, the stories say, Nanak went into the water and vanished.

teach.b: The janamsakhis, the old stories of Guru Nanak, tell of the morning he went to bathe in the Bein and vanished.
Tradition says he was gone for three days, and that when he came back, his first words were: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. This path told that story long ago. Today, the river itself.
In our own times the Kali Bein was choked with weeds and waste, and dirty water ran into it. The river of that story was hard to recognize.
Then volunteers began to clean it by kar seva, the Sikh name for free, hands-on work for a sacred place, the same kind of work that has cleaned the pools at gurdwaras.
A Sikh sant, Balbir Singh Seechewal, is known for leading it. They cleared weeds and silt by hand, worked on stopping the dirty water, and planted the banks. Over time, the water ran again.
The root is in the Asa di Var, at Ang 472, where Guru Nanak says that first of all, water is life, by which everything is made green.
If water is where life begins, a dirty river isn't only an eyesore. It's a wound in the place the Guru called life itself. So the volunteers treated it as seva, not a project.
The Guru disappeared into that water. They made sure there was water worth coming back out of.

how: Kar seva is volunteer labor for a sacred place, such as cleaning a gurdwara's sarovar or building and repairing gurdwaras. At Sultanpur Lodhi, volunteers have cleaned the Kali Bein by kar seva, and Sikhs visit the Gurdwara Ber Sahib there, linked with the story of Guru Nanak's disappearance in the river.

practice: If you can, set a glass of water in front of you and look at it.
Breathe in and think of where it came from, a river, a reservoir, rain on a hillside far away; breathe out and think of where it goes next, downstream to someone else, a field, a fish.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out, and then take one slow sip.
